newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Top Swedish companies seen spurning crown for euro.
newsitem.headline: Top Swedish companies seen spurning crown for euro.

text.p: Top Swedish firms may spurn the crown and embrace the euro when Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) starts in 1999, ignoring an expected government decision not to join the first wave of a single currency.

"Large companies will use the euro as their group currency," Bo Carlsson, economist at the Swedish Employers' Confederation, told Reuters. "If they aren't allowed to account in the euro, more companies might consider moving their headquarters abroad."

Sweden is widely expected to reject membership of EMU at its January, 1999 launch and opt instead to join at a later date. A decision on the issue from the ruling Social Democratic Party is expected next Tuesday.
One of Sweden's leading companies, telecoms group Ericsson, is thinking of heading abroad, citing a poor business climate and high tax pressure.
Other big groups will avoid emigration by tapping the benefits of EMU through subsidiaries already based within the European Union (EU).
"Large companies will be pulled along in the EMU project whether or not Sweden joins," Emil Ems, director at the Federation of Swedish Industries, said.
"The euro is a superior transaction currency and all payments from the continent, and maybe also from Eastern Europe, will be in the euro," he added.

Such companies may also begin borrowing from the freshly created euro-denominated capital markets, rather than in crowns, putting pressure on Swedish banks to offer euro-denominated products as well in order to keep their clients.
"The financial sector will be forced to offer companies services available in euro countries," Carlsson said.
Corporate accounting in terms of the euro would then follow naturally and the Federation of Swedish Industries has already called for a legislation changes that will make this possible.

Sweden's massive car maker Volvo is still considering the introduction of euro accounting for 1999 but already presents its income statement and balance sheet in both euro and crowns, spokesman Mats Edenborg said.
Drug maker Astra is forging ahead with plans to change over to the euro in order to iron out the problems presented by reporting in crown following it's recent volatility.
"It would mean large advantages for export companies to be able to account in a stable currrency," Astra spokesman Staffan Ternby said.
"We have double accounting now as we have to show figures both in crowns and in fixed foreign exchange rates as the crown has been so volatile. This is very troublesome."
With corporate Sweden signalling that it would embrace EMU, economists warned that the crown could easily become marginalised.

"The crown could become a volatile, trash currency, or a currency nobody cares about," said Carl Hamilton, chief economist at Handelsbanken. "But a link to ERM2 could counterbalace this," he added, referring to the prospect of Sweden joining a later wave of the single currency.
